terms.Mean squared error: MSE is the negative log-likelihood of a Gaussian noise model with fixed variance, which is why least squares is the maximum-likelihood fit under that assumption and why its optimal prediction is the conditional mean. It decomposes into squared bias plus error variance. Its gradient, proportional to the residual, lets a few large errors dominate training, and it is scale-dependent, so values are only comparable on the same target. RMSE restores units and always satisfies MAE <= RMSE <= sqrt(n) x MAE. For heteroscedastic data, a Gaussian NLL that also predicts variance is the principled upgrade.
terms.Mean absolute error: MAE corresponds to Laplace noise and is minimized by the conditional median, making it robust to outliers in the target but not to high-leverage points in the features. Its gradient is the sign of the residual, constant in size, so optimization near the optimum oscillates without learning-rate decay, and the loss has a kink at zero. Linear MAE regression can be solved exactly as a linear program. When the target distribution is skewed, a model trained on MAE predicts the median, which will look biased if judged by mean-based metrics such as MSE or aggregated totals.
terms.R-squared: R-squared = 1 - SS_res / SS_tot compares a model with the constant mean predictor. For OLS with an intercept on training data it lies in [0, 1] and equals the squared correlation between predictions and targets; on held-out data it can be negative. It depends on the spread of the target in the evaluation set, so the same model scores higher on a more varied population, which makes cross-dataset comparisons misleading. Training R-squared never decreases when features are added, which adjusted R-squared partially corrects. For model selection, cross-validated error is more reliable.
terms.Normalized discounted cumulative gain: DCG@k sums gains discounted by log2(rank + 1); the gain is either the relevance grade or 2^grade - 1, a choice that must be reported because scores differ. Dividing by the ideal DCG normalizes each query to [0, 1] so averages are meaningful. Computing the ideal from all known relevant items, not only retrieved ones, is stricter and standard. NDCG is the default offline metric for web search and recommendation, and LambdaMART optimizes it via pairwise gradients weighted by NDCG change. Its logarithmic discount is a convention; ERR and rank-biased precision use explicit user-patience models instead.
terms.Mean reciprocal rank: Reciprocal rank is 1/r for the first relevant item at rank r, or 0 if none appears within the cutoff. MRR suits tasks with one correct answer, such as question answering, code search or entity lookup, and is dominated by the first few positions. It ignores additional relevant results, so a system that finds one good item quickly scores the same as one that also finds five more. When each query has exactly one relevant item, MRR and MAP coincide. Significance testing should be done per query with a paired test, because MRR distributions are highly skewed.
terms.Expected calibration error: ECE bins predictions by confidence and averages |accuracy - confidence| weighted by bin size; maximum calibration error reports the worst bin. It is biased upward on small samples, sensitive to bin count and scheme (equal-width versus equal-mass), and not a proper scoring rule: predicting the base rate achieves ECE near zero while being useless. Report it alongside log loss or Brier score and a reliability diagram with bin counts. For multiclass models, distinguish top-label ECE from classwise ECE. Temperature scaling on a held-out set is the standard first remedy for high ECE in neural networks.
terms.Brier score: The Brier score is the mean squared error between predicted probabilities and binary outcomes. It is strictly proper, so honest probabilities minimize it in expectation. The Murphy decomposition splits it into reliability (calibration error), resolution (how informative predictions are) and uncertainty (base-rate variance). Unlike log loss it is bounded, so a single confident mistake costs at most 1, making it more tolerant of label noise. The Brier skill score compares it with the base-rate forecast, whose score is p(1 - p). Multiclass versions sum squared errors over the full probability vector.
terms.Statistical power: Power is 1 - beta, the probability of rejecting the null when a specified effect exists. It depends on alpha, sample size, metric variance and effect size; for proportions with alpha 0.05 and 80% power, n per arm is about 16 p(1 - p) / MDE^2, so halving the detectable effect quadruples the sample. Variance reduction such as CUPED raises power without more traffic. Underpowered studies are doubly harmful: they miss real effects, and the significant results they produce overstate effect sizes (the winner's curse). Post-hoc power computed from the observed effect adds no information beyond the p-value.
terms.Huber loss: Huber loss is quadratic for |e| <= delta and linear beyond, with matching value and slope at the joint, so its gradient is continuous and capped at delta in magnitude. In robust statistics it is an M-estimator; delta of about 1.345 noise standard deviations keeps 95% efficiency under Gaussian noise. Smooth L1, used for bounding-box regression, is Huber divided by delta. As delta grows the loss approaches half the MSE, and as it shrinks it approaches a scaled MAE. Pseudo-Huber and log-cosh are smooth everywhere. Delta is in target units, so retune it after rescaling targets.
terms.Focal loss: Introduced with the RetinaNet detector, focal loss is -alpha (1 - p_t)^gamma log p_t. With gamma = 2, an example at p_t = 0.9 keeps 1% of its cross-entropy, while hard examples keep most of theirs, so the flood of easy negatives in dense detection stops dominating the gradient. The paper also initializes the final bias to a low prior probability of about 0.01 for stability. Because it changes the loss minimizer, predicted probabilities are miscalibrated and should be recalibrated before use as probabilities. For tabular imbalance, class weights plus threshold tuning are often equally effective.
terms.InfoNCE: InfoNCE is cross-entropy over temperature-scaled similarities in which the positive must be identified among N candidates; minimizing it maximizes a lower bound on mutual information that cannot exceed log N. NT-Xent, from SimCLR, is the cosine-similarity version over 2N augmented views. Lower temperature concentrates gradients on hard negatives. Performance scales with the number of negatives, so large batches, cross-device gathering or momentum queues (MoCo) are common. CLIP applies it symmetrically over an image-text similarity matrix. False negatives from duplicates and semantic matches are the main failure mode; SigLIP swaps the softmax for per-pair sigmoids.
terms.Evidence lower bound: For a latent-variable model, log p(x) = ELBO + KL(q(z|x) || p(z|x)), so maximizing the ELBO tightens the bound and improves the approximate posterior at once. In a VAE the ELBO is a reconstruction log-likelihood minus KL(q(z|x) || p(z)), estimated with reparameterized samples z = mu + sigma * eps; the Gaussian KL has a closed form. Weighting the KL term gives beta-VAE. Posterior collapse occurs when the KL term goes to zero and the decoder ignores z. The simple noise-prediction loss of diffusion models is a reweighted form of a diffusion ELBO.
